title: Yet another "what AI game dev taught me" post (sorry)
author: yanenrogne
selftext:
This isn’t a showcase or anything. I’m not selling a game, there’s no link in the post. 

What actually surprised me is that AI didn’t really change how I write code, it changed how I make decisions.

Before AI, I’d spend days going back and forth on whether an idea was even worth trying.

Now I can just prototype it in an hour… and scrap it an hour later.

Funny enough, I’ve gotten less attached to my ideas because it’s so easy to test them. Coding takes seconds to minutes now, I feel less bad just letting it go. Figuring out what not to build is way harder than building it.

AI didn’t suddenly make me a better dev, it just made it way easier to realize when my ideas kinda suck lol

Go ahead and try your funny idea, heck try three different versions of it, don't be afraid 

Anyone else feel this shift? I feel it's crazy how we can navigate creativity without being held back by sunk cost fallacy (for time)

comments.author: Alstroph
comments.body:
I see it as hiring a fleet of contractors to work with you, except they do exactly what you want (for the most part). They’re above average skill wise, and ridiculously fast.

Human employment needs set aside, I am not really sure what the difference between hiring a contractor and utilizing AI is when it comes to ownership of your product.

comments.author: silly_bet_3454
comments.body:
Yeah it showed me (and to some extent even regular game dev on modern engines showed me this but especially with AI on top) that the raw coding of mechanics is not the hard part. Literally everything else is the hard part, art design, animations, testing, performance, having a good idea in the first place, marketing, etc. and I have like zero drive to really get deep into any of that stuff.

But in particular, what's crazy to me as an engineer getting into game dev is you realize, what actually makes games fun is not the underlying concept or even just the raw mechanics necessarily, but rather the million little details that make everything feel polished, like a finished product, a balanced game, an artistic vision seen through. All these things require a big team and huge investment and luck. AI helps with all that but only marginally IMO.

comments.author: Rude_Context_4844
comments.body: Ai changes a lot of things

comments.author: FocusKontrol
comments.body:
I’m finding that now my workflow is:  
1. thinking of an idea  
2. telling AI to implement it on top of my existing systems. 3. then I act as a QA/tester. Either improve it in some iterations or scrap it.  
And I can try a bunch of things that I did think of before but it would have taken way too long time to figure out how to implement it.
